Abstract: 47

Over the past few decades, the rising burden of metabolic disease including type 2 diabetes 48

mellitus (T2DM), pre-diabetes, obesity, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver 49

disease (MASLD) has corresponded with fundamental shifts in the landscape of heart failure 50

(HF) epidemiology, including the rising prevalence of heart failure with preserved ejection 51

fraction (HFpEF). It has become increasingly important to understand the role of extracardiac 52

contributors and inter-organ communication in the pathophysiology and phenotypic 53

heterogeneity of HF. Whereas traditional epidemiological strategies have separately examined 54

individual contributions of specific comorbidities to HF risk, these approaches may not capture 55

the shared mechanisms and more complex, bidirectional relationships between cardiac and non- 56

cardiac comorbidities. In this review, we highlight the cardiac, kidney, liver, and metabolism 57

multi-organ interactions and pathways that complicate HF development and progression and 58

propose research strategies to further understand HF in the context of multiple organ disease. 59

This includes evolving epidemiologic approaches such as multi-omics and machine learning 60

which may better capture common underlying mechanisms and inter-organ crosstalk. We review 61

existing preclinical models of HF and how they have enhanced our understanding of the role of 62

multi-organ disease in the development of HF subtypes. We suggest recommendations as to how 63

clinical practice across multiple specialties should screen for and manage multi-organ 64

involvement in HF. Finally, recognizing the advent of novel combinatorial therapeutic agents 65

which may have multiple indications across the cardiac-kidney-liver metabolism continuum, we 66

review the current clinical trials landscape. We specifically highlight a pressing need for the 67

design of more inclusive trials that examine the contributions of multimorbidity and incorporate 68

multi-organ endpoints, which we propose may lead to outcomes that are evermore clinically 69

relevant today. 70

INTRODUCTION 77

The incidence of heart failure (HF) is steadily increasing, with up to 1 in 4 individuals now 78

expected to develop HF in their lifetime1. This rise has been attributed to an increasing 79

prevalence of cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular comorbidities which may both contribute to 80

and complicate HF, ranging from obesity and related cardiometabolic risk factors to multiorgan 81

failure2,3. Moreover, as HF incidence increases, so does HF-related mortality, likely reflecting an 82

increased comorbidity burden amongst patients with HF4. Given these concerning trends, it is 83

increasingly important not only to identify patients at risk of HF, but also to comprehensively 84

map the contributions of cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular comorbidities to HF 85

development and progression. 86

87

Broadly, HF has been categorized into HF with preserved (pEF) vs reduced (rEF), based on left 88

ventricular ejection fraction. Presently, this distinction not only separates the subtypes by 89

echocardiographic appearance, but also by underlying etiology, epidemiology, and prognosis5. 90

Notwithstanding, the pattern of HF subtype epidemiology has changed substantially over the past 91

several decades, with the proportion of HFpEF increasing alongside the increasing global burden 92

of obesity6. In the last decade, HFpEF has overtaken HFrEF as the most common HF subtype 93

among incident cases7. The rising incidence of HFpEF in particular has further accentuated the 94

need to understand the role of obesity and extracardiac contributors to HF, as individuals with 95

HFpEF—in contrast to HFrEF—predominantly suffer from non-cardiovascular mortality8,9. 96

Thus, even beyond HF subtypes, consideration of multi-morbid and multi-organ contributions to 97

HF may help to resolve phenotypic heterogeneity. 98

99

In addition, despite advances in HF treatment, significant gaps remain in the clinical 100

management of comorbidities associated with HF and cardiometabolic disease10,11. Multi-organ 101

comorbidities not only exacerbate HF, but also complicate treatment, necessitating integrated 102

care strategies to manage both HF and its associated diseases10. Whereas the current foundation 103

of HF treatment is guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), which significantly improves 104

clinical outcomes and reduces mortality, these strategies are not tailored to the underlying 105

comorbidity burden or disease phenotype of a given individual. Given that HF mortality has 106

increased and treatment efficacy remains limited for advanced cases, it is increasingly important 107

to tailor strategies to individual patients, highlighting the need for the integration of multi- 108

morbidity into existing and future preclinical and clinical models. 109

110

In this review, we first tackle the traditional epidemiologic view by outlining individual 111

contributions of cardiometabolic comorbidities to HF, and we then highlight the complex 112

interactions of obesity and cardiometabolic disease with multiple organ systems and multi- 113

directional inter-organ crosstalk complicating HF development. Specifically, we review how 114

shared and distinct pathways contribute to the development of HFpEF vs HFrEF and examine 115

how multimorbidity contributes to each. We also review evolving epidemiologic approaches that 116

may overcome traditional ‘siloed’ views and propose a more complete and integrated 117

understanding of complex multi-morbid and multi-organ involvement in HF.  This includes the 118

incorporation of established and emerging biomarkers that capture multi-organ contributions to 119

HF and provide critical insights into phenotypic heterogeneity in both HFpEF and HFrEF. 120

Building on this premise, we also review existing and emerging preclinical models that 121

investigate multi-organ disease contributions to HF. Lastly, we review the current clinical trials 122

landscape and propose strategies to design and implement multi-morbidity trials to achieve 123

reliable and clinically relevant outcomes. 124

Individual Contributions of Comorbidities to Heart Failure: A Traditional Epidemiologic 126

Approach 127

128

Existing epidemiologic studies have largely focused on individual cardiometabolic risk factors 129

and their participation in HF pathophysiology, with multiple risk factors considered collectively 130

as additive contributions in multivariable risk prediction models. Each established HF risk factor 131

possesses shared and distinct contributions to the development of HFpEF vs HFrEF. In this 132

section, we first review individual comorbidities as they relate to HF, before integrating across 133

multiple comorbidities and proposing approaches to account for complex inter-organ crosstalk. 134

135

Age 136

HF is predominantly a disease of the elderly, with the lifetime risk of HF increasing to 38% by 137

age 9012. Whereas age itself likely does not cause HF in isolation, cardiovascular aging 138

substantially lowers the threshold for other risk factor-mediated cardiovascular changes through 139

a combination of autophagy, reduced cardiac regeneration, senescence, and oxidative stress13. In 140

one study of >130,000 Medicare beneficiaries, age was identified as the strongest predictor of 141

HF development across subtypes, with a “relative influence” of >35% as examined with a 142

gradient-boosted model14. While age is a major risk factor for all forms of HF, some studies 143

suggest greater age-related risk in the development of HFpEF vs HFrEF15. 144

145

Hypertension 146

Hypertension (HTN) is a primary driving factor in the development of both HFpEF and 147

HFrEF15,16. In the Framingham Heart Study (FHS), HTN predated the development of HF in 148

91% of all patients diagnosed with HF over 20 years of follow-up, with a mean of 12 years of 149

antecedent HTN; this translates to a 39% population attributable risk (PAR) for HF in men and 150

59% in women17. HTN and arterial stiffness directly contribute to both systolic and diastolic 151

ventricular dysfunction through the development of left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy13. Left 152

untreated, pathological cardiac remodeling and/or overt clinical HF are expected consequences 153

of the natural history of HTN16, and conversely, antihypertensive treatment has been shown to 154

prevent HF18. 155

156

Diabetes 157

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) has been consistently associated with ~2-4-fold increased risk of 158

HF, with augmented risk observed in the setting of worsening glycemic control19,20. A total of 159

28% of all patients with T2D ultimately develop HFrEF, and 25% develop HFpEF21. 160

Cardiovascular risk associated with T2D is largely attributed to the macrovascular, 161

microvascular, and inflammatory complications of hyperglycemia and insulin resistance22. In 162

addition, T2D is associated with cardiac remodeling, ranging from increases in LV mass, relative 163

wall thickness, left atrial (LA) size, and the presence of diastolic dysfunction, even prior to the 164

development of clinical disease23,24. In keeping with this broad array of cardiovascular effects, 165

T2D is a prominent risk factor for both HFpEF and HFrEF15. 166

167

Obesity 168


<!-- Page 6 -->


Obesity is both a strong independent risk factor for HF itself as well as a distinct risk factor for a 169

host of other cardiometabolic diseases that contribute to HF in turn, ranging from hypertension 170

and diabetes to coronary artery disease25. In the FHS, each one-unit increase in body mass index 171

(BMI) was associated with a 5% higher risk of HF in men and 7% in women, with similar 172

findings observed across Finland, the Physicians Health Study, among many others26-28. Obesity 173

may lead to HF through direct cardiac effects, ranging from cardiomyocyte hypertrophy to 174

fibrosis, in addition to systemic processes such as inflammation and endothelial dysfunction25,29. 175

Whereas these effects may contribute to the development of both HF subtypes, obesity is 176

especially central to HFpEF development5. This hypothesis is corroborated by a pooled analysis 177

of WHI, MESA, and CHS, that demonstrated that higher BMI was associated with both HF 178

subtypes, but with a more consistent dose-response relationship with HFpEF rather than HFrEF 179

risk30,31. Importantly, the differential risk of obesity and risk of future HFpEF vs HFrEF appears 180

particularly pronounced among women relative to men32. 181

182

Chronic Kidney Disease 183

Whereas the many contributions of diverse organ systems to HF risk are well described, the 184

association between chronic kidney disease (CKD) and HF is best established in traditional 185

epidemiologic studies. CKD likely contributes to HF development via a combination of vascular 186

calcification and remodeling, neurohormonal disruption, and myocardial fibrosis and 187

remodeling33. Across three large community cohorts, the presence of CKD was associated with 188

increased risk of HF similar in magnitude to that of coronary heart disease34. Indeed, other 189

indicators of CKD such as albuminuria are also independently associated with incident HF 190

diagnosis and prognosis35. CKD is one of the most common comorbidities in HF patients, with a 191

slightly higher prevalence in the Swedish Heart Study among those with HFpEF (56%) than 192

HFrEF (45%) 36. This observation was corroborated in a prospective study of >3,500 individuals 193

with CKD and no prevalent HF37, that identified a higher incidence of new HFpEF vs HFrEF 194

hospitalizations. 195

196

Other Subtype-Specific Risk Factors 197

The overall lifetime risk of HF is comparable between sexes, yet important sex differences have 198

been noted, with greater prevalence of HFpEF reported among women compared with men38. 199

The complex relationship of female sex with HFpEF development is an area of active 200

investigation, with potential contributions from underlying differences in cardiometabolic traits, 201

hormonal changes, markers of inflammation and fibrosis, exercise capacity, and cardiac 202

mechanics39-41. Conversely, smoking, high cholesterol, and left bundle branch block have all 203

been identified as stronger risk factors for HFrEF, which may reflect contributions to the 204

development of coronary artery disease and subsequent ischemic cardiomyopathy15,42-44. In 205

addition, the presence of underlying coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, and 206

arrhythmia both contribute to and share risk factors with both HFpEF and HFrEF, but these 207

associations lie beyond the scope of this overview given our focus on underlying 208

cardiometabolic contributions to HF. 209

210

Combining Individual Comorbidities to Estimate HF Risk 211

A number of risk prediction scores exist, each of which combine information across comorbid 212

conditions and risk factors to estimate future risk of HF. The use of risk assessment tools was 213

extensively reviewed previously by the American Heart Association and the American College 214


<!-- Page 7 -->


of Cardiology45,46. For example, race- and sex-specific 10-year-risk equations for HF were 215

derived and validated, utilizing an individual’s age, blood pressure, glucose, BMI, cholesterol, 216

smoking status, and QRS duration to capture their cardiometabolic risk47. The Health ABC and 217

Framingham risk scores similarly integrate traditional risk factors with additional physical and 218

laboratory data (i.e., heart rate, creatinine, albumin, and the presence of left ventricular 219

hypertrophy or cardiomegaly) to estimate risk48,49, while the Atherosclerosis Risk in 220

Communities (ARIC) risk score additionally incorporates the predictive power of natriuretic 221

peptides,50 Most recently, the American Heart Association’s PREVENT equations estimate 222

absolute 10-year risk of incident HF using a base model (age, sex, total and HDL cholesterol, 223

systolic BP, BMI, eGFR, T2D, current smoking, anti-hypertensive medication, lipid lowering 224

medication), as well as the optional addition of urinary albumin-to-creatine ratio, estimated 225

glomerular filtration rate, hemoglobin A1c, and social deprivation index to further refine risk 226

assessment51. 227

228

However, whereas these HF risk prediction models approximate risk, they do not yet 229

comprehensively capture other important factors known to contribute to HF development, 230

ranging from metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), obstructive 231

sleep apnea, physical inactivity and skeletal muscle dysfunction, to immune activation and 232

inflammation52-54. Further, in clinical practice, risk calculators are a useful population broad- 233

based tool for disease prevention and prediction; however, we still lack patient-level precision to 234

distinguish disease subtypes or the nuanced contributions of different comorbidities to HF 235

development. As we refine our understanding of HF pathogenesis and disease heterogeneity, we 236

propose that it is critical to consider a) potential bidirectional associations between HF 237

development and comorbidities, b) shared mechanisms of disease leading to HF and other extra- 238

cardiac manifestations of cardiometabolic disease, and c) the role of inter-organ crosstalk in HF 239

development and progression. 240

241

Multiorgan Failure in HF: Shared Mechanisms and/or Reciprocal Risk? 242

243

When examining the contribution of cardiometabolic risk factors to HF and extra-cardiac organ 244

dysfunction, it is important to recognize that a) shared mechanisms may lead to parallel 245

development of cardiac and extra-cardiac disease and b) interorgan crosstalk may contribute to 246

bidirectional risk, compounding and accelerating the development of multimorbidity55. This 247

concept of complex inter-organ interactions is exemplified by the reciprocal risk observed 248

between CKD and HF (Figure 1). 249

250

It is well established that cardiometabolic risk factors such as obesity, diabetes, and HTN 251

contribute separately to the development of both CKD and HF in parallel56. These comorbidities 252

underlie both disease processes and likely represent a “common soil” for the development of 253

both cardiac and kidney dysfunction, mediated by the development of microvascular dysfunction 254

and inflammation33. Moreover, as discussed above, CKD is an independent risk factor for the 255

development of both incident HFpEF and HFrEF36,37. In turn, HF is an independent risk factor 256

for both the development and progression of CKD. Up to 65-70% of individuals with end-stage 257

kidney disease have prevalent HF57, and HF is associated with a 2x higher risk of incident 258

CKD58. Thus, in addition to the shared “common soil” of cardiometabolic risk factors, reciprocal 259

inter-organ interactions between the heart and kidney further compound and accelerate multi- 260

Shared Pathophysiologic Mechanisms and Inter-organ Crosstalk 265

Individual chapters in this Compendium will address the specific interactions of different organs 266

with HF, the key features of which are summarized in Table 1.  At the same time, it is important 267

to highlight the common pathways of pathophysiology that may underlie many forms of multi- 268

organ dysfunction, including cardiometabolic disease, genetics, and inflammation. 269

270

The widespread consequences of cardiometabolic disease include alterations in adipocyte 271

signaling, myokines, hepatokines, secreted gastrointestinal and endocrine factors, and vascular 272

factors; each of these alterations may contribute to the development of HF, other organ 273

dysfunction, and the interactions between the two59,60. Inter-organ crosstalk may also be 274

mediated by genetic traits shared between HF and other underlying cardiometabolic risk factors, 275

such as blood pressure and dysglycemia61. Five genes were recently identified as potential 276

mediators of crosstalk between HF and CKD and may be involved in disease progression for 277

both processes62. Similar shared associations have also been identified for the liver-heart axis63, 278

as well as between COPD and other forms of cardiovascular disease64. 279

280

Importantly, local and systemic inflammation is hypothesized to play a role in the development 281

of both HF and other chronic kidney, liver, and lung diseases, with the paradigm of HFpEF, for 282

example, increasingly shifting toward one of systemic inflammation as a common underlying 283

cause of myocardial fibrosis, endothelial dysfunction, and multimorbidity65,66. Multiple 284

mediators of inflammation, ranging from protein biomarkers to eicosanoid metabolites, have 285

been associated with both incident and prevalent HF67,68. As reviewed, heightened inflammatory 286

activity may also separately contribute to kidney69, lung70, liver71 and other multiorgan disease in 287

parallel, or else as a result of the inflammatory cascade spurred by HF development. As such, 288

biochemical profiling is critical to fully understand these molecular mechanisms of HF 289

pathophysiology itself as well as inter-organ crosstalk, as discussed below. In addition, given the 290

emerging evidence for anti-inflammatory therapy for individuals with chronic HF, these shared 291

mechanisms of inflammation may also represent key opportunities for both prevention and 292

treatment of multi-organ morbidity72. 293

294

Evolving Approaches to HF Epidemiology: Capturing Inter-Organ Interplay 295

A Multi-Organ Approach to HF Epidemiology 296

Whereas it may be simpler to focus on the separate contributions of each individual organ system 297

to HF risk, a more integrated approach (as proposed in Figure 2) instead considers the 298

development of HF as the progression from an initial, “inciting insult” to clinical disease via a 299

spectrum of shared pathways mediated by inter-organ interplay. In HFpEF, this “inciting insult” 300

is most commonly obesity, whereas in HFrEF, this insult may be the exposure to a genetic, 301

autoimmune/inflammatory, or ischemic trigger for the development of cardiomyopathy. After the 302

initial insult or trigger, disease presentation is further modulated via “common soil” factors such 303

as obesity and cardiometabolic disease that may lead to multi-organ dysfunction, coupled with 304

inter-organ crosstalk, that together act like a “prism” and diverge into multiple HF 305

subphenotypes and clinical presentations. In other words, cardiometabolic risk factors and the 306


<!-- Page 9 -->


shared pathophysiology of inflammation, fibrosis, and metabolic dysregulation lead to HF and 307

multi-organ dysfunction, with inter-organ crosstalk magnifying the “spectrum” of clinical 308

presentation and multimorbidity. 309

310

Whereas prior studies have examined associations of each individual comorbid condition with 311

HF, future epidemiologic studies should consider HF risk not only as a concatenation of 312

individual risk factors, but also as an integration of shared mechanisms and multi-organ 313

interplay. These approaches are enabled by technological advances in molecular profiling of 314

disease, large consortia, studies spanning epidemiology and real-world HF samples, and 315

emerging computational methods designed to analyze multi-dimensional datasets, as outlined 316

below. 317

318

BIOMARKERS 319

Assessing Multi-Organ Involvement in Heart Failure using Biomarkers 320

Biochemical profiling has greatly advanced our understanding of HF pathophysiology, 321

prediction, and management. In addition to risk prediction and prognostication specific to HF, 322

biochemical profiling also has the potential to provide insights into multi-organ involvement and 323

inter-organ crosstalk as it relates to HF. Shared driver pathways in MASLD have also 324

highlighted its multiorgan consequences of poor cardiovascular-liver metabolic health. Early 325

identification of at-risk individuals with MASLD may therefore also support identifying those at 326

higher risk of HF. The role of biomarkers in HF has been extensively reviewed previously73, and 327

a list of well-studied biomarkers across multiple organs with their interplay with the heart is 328

summarized in Figure 3. 329

330

Established and emerging HF blood biomarkers 331

Natriuretic peptides are the most well-defined biomarkers of HF and remain the strongest 332

predictor of adverse cardiovascular events, regardless of obesity status74. Given the known 333

effects of other chronic diseases on natriuretic peptide values, including natriuretic peptide 334

deficiency phenotype in obesity, clinical guidelines to interpret natriuretic peptides in these 335

settings have been laid out by the Heart Failure Association of the European Society of 336

Cardiology75. Given the complexity of HF, no single biomarker is comprehensive, and additional 337

markers have been found to add incremental value to NT-proBNP. For example, two extra- 338

cardiac biomarkers – soluble ST2 (sST2) and galectin-3 – have been listed with Class IIb 339

recommendations in European and American HF clinical guidelines in addition to their roles in 340

tissue fibrosis76,77. Beyond their utility in HF prognosis and risk stratification, they are also listed 341

biomarkers of chronic kidney disease, which frequently coexist with HF. In addition to the broad 342

array of established protein biomarkers of myocardial remodeling, fibrosis, and inflammation 343

listed in Figure 3, there are also numerous emerging non-protein biomarkers with important 344

value to HF prediction and prognosis. For example, exosomes carrying MicroRNAs (miRNAs) 345

such as miR-210-3p, miR-23a-3p, and miR-221-3p have been shown to predict HF 346

hospitalizations and progression78. Differentially regulated miRNA profiles also bear potential 347

diagnostic utility for subgrouping of HFpEF and HFrEF subtypes79. However, given the complex 348

regulatory role of miRNA, the extra-cardiac effects of circulating HF miRNAs in HF 349

development remain to be explored. However, emerging evidence suggests that extra-cardiac 350

biomarkers—including miRNA—may mediate crosstalk among different organs over the course 351

of heart failure development, perpetuating multi-organ disease severity and affecting the 352


<!-- Page 10 -->


interpretability of advanced-stage diseases. For example, a commonly upregulated miR-21 in 353

HF, can perpetuate kidney injury through the silencing of metabolic genes80.  Other non-protein 354

biomarkers of particular relevance to inter-organ cross-talk include metabolites such as N- 355

formylanthranilic acid, which serves as a marker of both HFpEF risk and chronic kidney disease 356

and function81. These connections further highlight the potential systemic implications of 357

secreted factors across CKLM sectors, which may provide insight into the underpinnings of 358

multi-organ disease development and progression. 359

Utility of multi-marker approaches 360

Numerous studies have examined the use of multiple biomarkers to refine risk prediction and 361

characterize patients with specific HF phenotypes. For example, in a prospective study of the 362

HELPFul cohort82, investigators examined the association of clinical phenogroups with 32 363

distinct biomarkers. GDF-15, along with NT-proBNP, matrix metalloproteinase, insulin-like 364

growth factor-binding proteins, and osteoprotegerin were among the top biomarkers to separate 365

the HFpEF phenogroups, suggesting that these circulating biomarker profiles may both delineate 366

the role of key processes of HFpEF pathophysiology in disease classification as well as 367

potentially inform strategies for early intervention. Moreover, another multi-biomarker plasma 368

study in TOPCAT trial participants also revealed a combination of biomarkers related to key 369

HFpEF pathophysiology with enhanced risk stratification of HFpEF using a machine learning 370

method termed the Tree-based pipeline optimization tool (TPOT)83.  Hence, the combinatorial 371

deployment of biomarkers and machine learning strategies might indeed offer discrimination of 372

HFpEF subtypes and patient risk outcomes. 373

Assessing kidney health in MASLD HF patients using serum and urinary-based cardiorenal 375

biomarkers 376

MASLD is generally associated with higher risk of CKD and cardiovascular disease, with 377

clinical consensus now advocating for assessment of comorbidities including kidney disease in 378

these patients84. eGFR and albuminuria are classical markers of kidney dysfunction, among a 379

growing list of inflammatory and kidney injury markers available now to better predict kidney 380

disease progression with metabolic risk implications85. The combined use of renal biomarkers, 381

such as cystatin-C, kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminidase (NAG), 382

neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), and osteopontin, could enhance the 383

prediction of pathways in CKD patients with MASLD at risk of HF. However, the clinical utility 384

of including the multiple, existing kidney biomarkers described85 may not be cost-effective and 385

practical, requiring further evaluation with other non-renal biomarkers in a multiorgan 386

assessment.  For example, besides classical eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) 387

measurements as seen in the DAPA-HF trial86, the use of a cardiorenal panel comprising NT- 388

proBNP, hs-cTnT, GDF-15, and IGFBP7 has been reported in the CREDENCE trial to convey 389

strong prognostic value for individuals with cardiorenal and metabolic risks87, further supporting 390

the prognostic utility of multi-marker approaches. In the subsequent sections below, we will also 391

discuss the integration of liver-specific endpoints into CKM trials in the Clinical Trials section, 392

and incorporating metabolic non-invasive tests (NITs) into cardiorenal studies. 393

Assessing liver health in MASLD HF patients using multiorgan non-invasive test (NITs) panels 395

396


<!-- Page 11 -->


Shared pathophysiology between MASLD and cardiovascular diseases calls for recognizing 397

MASLD as an important cardiovascular risk factor, and including indices of MASLD into future 398

HF risk assessment tools88. Second-line classical serum-based NITs include enhanced liver 399

fibrosis (ELF), and Fibrotest (combination of alpha-2-macroglobulin (A2M), haptoglobin, 400

apolipoprotein A1, GGT, total bilirubin, and ALT), as well as imaging-based NITs such as the 401

Liver Fibroscan (Transient Elastography), have been reviewed extensively elsewhere89. As liver 402

fibrosis is a strong predictor of cardiovascular outcomes, the incorporation of fibrosis scores, 403

such as the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) Index takes advantage of information derived from liver enzymes 404

- alanine transaminase (ALT), and aspartate transaminase (AST) – plus age and platelet counts, 405

the most validated to date for identifying individuals with liver fibrosis90. New NITs (FIB-9, 406

FIB-11, and FIB-12) with additional blood biomarkers have improved predictive accuracy 407

relative to conventional NITs91. Additionally, the recent discovery of three novel fibrotic 408

markers, IGFBP7, SSc5D, and Sema4D, that outperform existing NITs is promising92. From a 409

phenotyping perspective, advances in metabolic indices will likely aid in identifying patients 410

with liver fibrosis in a CVD population that harbors a combination of cardiorenal biomarkers, 411

which could be extended beyond liver endpoints. Given the cost-benefit of NITs, they are likely 412

to be useful for early risk stratification and screening for MASLD and can be combined with 413

cardiorenal biomarkers in HF cohorts. These may include the Fibroscan or FIB-4 with Cystatin C 414

or KIM-1, or cardio-hepatic panels integrating hsCRP, and FIB-4/ELF scores93. Importantly, it is 415

acknowledged that leveraging NITs to derive liver endpoints in cardiovascular or renal trials still 416

requires longitudinal validation due to its inherent variability.  Furthermore, there is no single 417

consensus NIT yet94.  The incorporation of liver endpoints and their limitations will be discussed 418

further in the Clinical Trials section below. 419

Multi-Omic and Multi-Organ Integration: Emerging Techniques 421

Evolving technologies enable large-scale -omic profiling across genetic variants, transcripts, 422

proteins and metabolites, as well as across different tissue types and cohorts. One recent study 423

utilized a systems biology approach to uncover markers for liver/heart interorgan interplay95, 424

serving as a useful example for future studies of HF development. The authors used several 425

strategies to capture inter-organ crosstalk, beginning by assessing the correlations between 426

transcriptomic data across different tissues and subsequently examining transcriptional findings 427

across the plasma proteome in a HFpEF preclinical model. Findings were then validated in 428

human datasets, identifying a series of novel biomarkers and pathways implicated as potential 429

mediators in the liver-heart bidirectional exchange. A similar recent analysis linked the 430

circulating proteome to clinical echocardiographic phenotyping and transcriptional myocardial 431

profiling in order to identify and prioritize markers for HF risk96. Other strategies have been 432

employed to manage high-dimensional data across different -omic platforms. For instance, cross- 433

integrative genomics allow for the integration of -omics analyses between diseases and traits97, 434

and trans-omics may be used to examine the network of differentially regulated metabolic 435

processes across multiple tissue types, revealing underlying dysregulated inter-organ metabolic 436

cycles98. In summary, emerging approaches of multi-omic and multi-organ integration may 437

facilitate the capture and refinement of HF risk from the perspective of multimorbidity by 438

integrating biological mediators across different tissue types and disease models. 439

Many of the novel multi-omics methods outlined above can aid in our understanding of HF 442

diverse multi-organ comorbidities and overlapping phenotypes, necessitating a systems biology 444

approach for precise, personalized assessment. A decade ago, Shah et al.99 pioneered the first 445

phenomapping effort in a HFpEF cohort, utilizing clinical, laboratory, and cardiac imaging 446

parameters as inputs for a supervised machine learning algorithm based on support vector 447

machines (SVM). This approach classified the heterogeneous HFpEF cohort into three distinct 448

phenogroups, with significant differences in survival free of cardiovascular hospitalization or 449

mortality and markedly different in terms of risk profiles and clinical manifestations. Since then, 450

numerous phenomapping efforts have used different data elements, including big data multi- 451

omics, and statistical tools, also extensively reviewed elsewhere100. 452

Although all three HFpEF phenogroups – a ‘metabolically obese phenotype’, a ‘young obese 454

with low natriuretic peptide phenotype’, and ‘the vascular aging phenotype’, bear different 455

clinical, proteomic, and transcriptomic profiles, they each have a set of unique contributions. For 456

example, the ‘metabolically obese phenotype,’ representing a third of HFpEF, has a high 457

prevalence of CKD and elevated levels of systemic inflammation marked by TNF-α, 458

interleukins, and GDF-15, which are also common to the development of both disease 459

processes101-103. Elevated markers of liver fibrosis such as YKL-40 also implicate the 460

contribution of liver-heart crosstalk to this phenogroup. Elevated inflammatory markers are also 461

similarly observed in the ‘vascular aging’ phenotype133. 462

463

To elucidate the biological pathways and mechanistic drivers for therapeutics in these 464

phenogroups, Hahn and colleagues leveraged both myocardial metabolomics and transcriptomics 465

to perform agnostic clustering of distinct metabolomic and transcriptomic signatures of HFpEF 466

subgroups63,64. Interestingly, the highest risk, ‘metabolically obese phenotype’ displayed an 467

activated stress-mediated kinase pathway profile, and metabolomic analysis revealed differences 468

in branched-chain amino acid catabolites and methylhistidine levels104. While the study hints at 469

metabolic and cellular pathway underpinnings of HFpEF subgroups, its correlation to proteomics 470

is still unknown, and many clinical comorbidities may have been excluded due to limited donors. 471

472

The systems biology approach was also deployed in the more homogeneous HFrEF multicentre 473

trial (BIOSTAT-CHF) across 11 European Countries105. Using a gradient-boosting machine- 474

learning strategy, the authors integrated 54 clinical phenotypes, 403 circulating plasma proteins, 475

blood transcriptomes, and genomic markers to model all-cause mortality across 2,516 patients, 476

discovering that decreased ERBB2 signaling may be implicated in all-cause mortality. 477

478

Taken together, whereas the traditional approach to HF epidemiology considers individual 479

contributions of different cardiometabolic disease risk factors to overall HF risk, shared 480

mechanisms, as well as concurrent extra-cardiac multiorgan dysfunction, quite clearly compound 481

HF risk (See Box 1). Cross-organ interplay may in fact be both bidirectional and nonlinear, 482

reflecting diseases developing in parallel or as a consequence of one another. Future studies to 483

integrate ‘common soil’ mechanisms from shared inciting insults with multi-organ involvement 484

and inter-organ crosstalk will allow us to fully elucidate multimorbidity and disease 485

heterogeneity across the spectrum of clinical HF. 486

PRECLINICAL MODELS 488

Traditional epidemiologic approaches are only a first step of many in the process of elucidating 489

the role of inter-organ crosstalk in heart failure. Whereas studies examining circulating 490

biomarkers provide invaluable insights into the mechanisms underlying heart failure, pre-clinical 491

models offer the opportunity to test these hypotheses in a mechanistic context. In addition, 492

animal models may interrogate established associations between the 'common soil' of underlying 493

cardiometabolic comorbidities and the onset of more complex organ failure, dissecting the stages 494

of disease progression and potential causality106,107. These studies take on particular importance 495

in the setting of multi-morbidity and the bidirectional risks between heart failure and other 496

chronic diseases, as described above. In this section, we will provide an overview of the existing 497

pre-clinical models of heart failure, including both HFrEF and HFpEF, and discuss opportunities 498

to develop future models to best capture the spectrum of inter-organ crosstalk in HF development 499

and progression. 500

Preclinical Models of HFrEF 502

Pathophysiological Mechanisms of HFrEF 503

HFrEF, typically caused by hypertension or myocardial infarction, is marked by impairment of 504

the ejection of blood108. The subsequent compensatory neurohormonal activation, such as via the 505

renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system, further 506

exacerbate HF symptoms109. Resulting pathophysiology involves changes in myocardial 507

remodeling, including ventricular dilation, fibrosis, and alterations in myocyte function110. These 508

mechanisms lead to additional decrease in the ability of the heart to pump blood efficiently, 509

contributing to hallmark symptoms of HFrEF, such as shortness of breath, fatigue, and fluid 510

retention. Here, we provide a brief overview of HFrEF mechanisms and models, focusing more 511

on HFpEF. 512

513

Defining HFrEF in Animal Models 514

Defining HFrEF in animal models is relatively straightforward as compared with HFpEF, 515

primarily relying on transthoracic echocardiographic indices such as reduced ejection fraction, 516

fractional shortening, and increased LV mass. Pathological assessment involves evaluating tissue 517

morphology, including features such as LV dilation, altered LV wall thickness, concentric or 518

eccentric LV hypertrophy, cardiomyocyte loss, and fibrosis, coupled with molecular markers of 519

fetal gene program re-activation. 520

521

Common HFrEF Models 522

The transverse aortic constriction (TAC) model is widely used for studying pathophysiological 523

mechanisms of HFrEF, first introduced in 1991 by Rockman and colleagues111,112. The primary 524

procedure involves anesthetizing the mouse, performing a thoracotomy to expose and isolate the 525

aorta, and then ligating it to create an artificial constriction with a diameter of approximately 0.4 526

mm113. This increases afterload on the left ventricle, promoting ventricular hypertrophy and 527

fibrosis, contractile dysfunction, and triggering a certain degree of inflammation. Ultimately, 528

these changes lead to ventricular dilation and the development of HFrEF112. The phenotype can 529

vary depending on specific aspects of the surgical procedure (e.g. positioning of the surgical 530

needle that dictates the degree of stenosis), the species and strain of experimental animals and the 531

timing of the intervention112,114. 532

533


<!-- Page 14 -->


Coronary artery ligation is another commonly used approach for inducing HFrEF. The principle 534

behind this model is surgically occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery to induce 535

myocardial infarction, causing myocardial cell death artificially, leading to impaired myocardial 536

contractile function and left ventricular remodeling, hallmarks of clinical HFrEF115-117.  Beyond 537

that, in most high-income countries, due to the widespread use of coronary reperfusion 538

approaches, acute myocardial infarction is typically followed by emergent reperfusion therapy, 539

and simple myocardial infarction is less commonly seen. Instead, the combination of ischemia 540

coupled with reperfusion injury causes damage to myocardial cells, leading to HFrEF118,119. 541

Therefore, a model involving temporary (e.g., 45 minutes) left anterior descending coronary 542

artery occlusion followed by a period of reperfusion (e.g., 24 hours) can be arguably more 543

accurate reflection of the clinical realities experienced by many patients, aligning more closely 544

with the pathophysiological process of HFrEF commonly seen in clinical practice today. 545

Pulmonary artery banding (PAB) can induce right ventricular (RV) dilation, right atrial 546

enlargement, and tricuspid regurgitation, leading to a reduction in RV ejection fraction120. 547

548

CKD models, including angiotensin II (Ang II) infusion, high-salt diet, and unilateral 549

nephrectomy, serve as valuable models for studying HFrEF by replicating the intricate interplay 550

between cardiac and renal dysfunction. Unilateral nephrectomy simulates renal dysfunction by 551

reducing nephron numbers, triggering compensatory mechanisms such as glomerular 552

hyperfiltration, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) activation, and progressive renal 553

damage. Collectively, these models capture the bidirectional relationship between CKD and 554

HFrEF, enabling researchers to investigate the underlying mechanisms of cardiorenal 555

comorbidities and evaluate therapeutic interventions targeting this complex 556

interconnection121,122. 557

558

Additionally, doxorubicin and alcohol are known to induce systemic damage, thereby mimicking 559

some of the key pathophysiological mechanisms associated with HFrEF. These drugs exert 560

widespread systemic effects that complicate the interpretation of results and reduce the 561

specificity of these models in isolating the cardiac effects of HFrEF121. 562

563

Finally, some studies employ genetically modified mice, such as nesprin-1 and Mybpc3-mutant 564

mice, to model HFrEF. By isolating specific genetic alterations associated with HFrEF, 565

transgenic models contribute to a deeper understanding of the syndrome and help refine 566

treatment approaches123,124. 567

Recently, two diagnostic algorithms—the HFA-PEFF125 and H₂ FPEF126 scores—that 570

incorporate typical clinical manifestations and comorbidities have been introduced to enhance 571

the accuracy of HFpEF diagnosis and prognosis. Although these scores are not perfect, they can 572

be used to evaluate the similarities between human HFpEF and animal models, thereby 573

Defining HFpEF in Preclinical Models 576

Pulmonary congestion 577

Wet-to-dry lung weight ratio at sacrifice is a simple index of pulmonary vasculature congestion 578

and helpful for establishing increased LV filling pressures129,130. 579

580

Exercise intolerance 581

Events underlying exercise intolerance in HFpEF are multifactorial, including LVDD, obesity, 582

pulmonary dysfunction, skeletal muscle weakness, and more. Voluntary or forced exercise 583

protocols (e.g. treadmill or swimming exercise) are commonly employed131. 584

585

Increased natriuretic peptide levels 586

Elevated natriuretic peptides, such as BNP and NT-proBNP, are responses to increased LV end- 587

diastolic pressure and wall stress, and are now integral to the diagnostic criteria for HFpEF in 588

humans132,133. Similarly, natriuretic peptide levels can be measured in plasma or LV tissue, where 589

they can afford complementary insights. However, comorbid conditions such as AF, obesity, and 590

kidney dysfunction can impact peptide levels in these models, complicating their interpretation. 591

592

Preserved systolic function 593

Systolic function should be preserved as validated by transthoracic echocardiography. In 594

addition, global longitudinal strain (GLS) is a crucial tool for assessing cardiac contractile 595

function, particularly in HFpEF, where GLS can uncover early functional declines characteristic 596

of HFpEF even when the ejection fraction remains within normal limits. GLS reflects the heart's 597

overall contractile function by measuring contractile strain. It can capture subtle changes in the 598

heart more sensitively than traditional ejection fraction and is highly significant in the early 599

diagnosis of HFpEF134,135. However, GLS results are subject to considerable variability, being 600

heavily influenced by heart rate and loading conditions. 601

602

Impaired diastolic function 603

Diastolic function should be evaluated and quantified by Doppler echocardiography. Elevated 604

E/e’ and diminished E/A ratios in Doppler ultrasound are indicative of LV diastolic dysfunction. 605

These parameters, however, vary across animal models, with E/e′ typically ranging from 10–16 606

and E/A from 1.0–2.5136. Additional markers, such as prolonged isovolumetric relaxation time 607

(IVRT), constant τ (tau), and reduced dP/dtmin, reflect delayed relaxation of LV cardiomyocytes 608

and further support the diagnosis of LVDD136,137. Notably, while E/e′ and E/A are highly heart 609

rate-dependent and can be challenging to measure consistently, IVRT is heart rate-independent, 610

offering a more stable and reliable parameter. 611

612

RPLSR (reverse peak longitudinal strain rate) measures the rate of myocardial deformation 613

during early diastole and serves as a sensitive marker for early-stage LVDD136,137. Like GLS, 614

RPLSR is highly dependent on imaging quality and heart rate, which introduces variability and 615

complicates standardization. 616

Hemodynamic assessment 618

Although invasive hemodynamic measurements are considered the gold standard for defining 619

HFpEF, their use in patients is limited due to their invasiveness and associated risks. These 620

procedures are also uncommon in rodent models but are frequently performed in large animal 621

models. Such measurements via LV pressure-volume loops and measurements of pulmonary 622

artery pressure provide valuable information, making them particularly useful as evaluating 623

clinical signs and symptoms in animals is challenging. 624

Preclinical Models of Comorbidities in HF and CMDs 665

In real-world clinical practice, and as elaborated above thus far, HF and its associated metabolic 666

comorbidities do not manifest as isolated components of inter-organ crosstalk, but rather as 667

interconnected and multifaceted conditions53,55,61,88,95. The heterogeneous nature and complex 668

pathophysiology in humans have to be taken into account when creating and validating animal 669

models116,128,136. We advocate for a broader, high-level perspective that synthesizes insights into 670

both HFrEF and HFpEF, culminating in a clear call to action for advancing research and clinical 671

management. 672

673

To better define human HF population, clinical parameters and comorbidity patterns, including 674

epidemiology, symptoms, echocardiography and laboratory indexes, treatment strategies, and 675

prognosis, are being used to cluster HF patients into distinct multimorbidity groups using latent 676

class analysis143-145. The common subgroups: (1) ischemic, often associated with atherosclerosis- 677

related risk factors and typically linked to HFrEF; (2) metabolic, frequently involving multiple 678

CMDs and presenting as HFpEF; (3) elderly individuals, often with AF; and (4) young, obese 679

individuals with minimal comorbidities. In parallel, recent advances have moved beyond 680

traditional unifactorial disease models, emphasizing the development of preclinical models that 681

capture the diverse clinical subtypes of HF and its associated comorbidities116,136. In the 682

following section, we focus on the multifactorial animal models in above-mentioned clinical HF 683

subtypes with different comorbidity patterns. 684

Ischemic Phenotype in HFrEF 685

Ischemic heart disease (IHD) is still arguably the most common etiology of HF, accounting for 686

approximately 40% of cases worldwide146,147. Clinically, patients with ischemic HF are often 687

male and frequently have risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and 688

peripheral artery disease. They are more likely to present with HFrEF and have a lower 689

prevalence of CKD143,145. Although myocardial infarction (MI) in patients is commonly caused 690

by the abrupt rupture, or erosion, of atherosclerotic plaques resulting from chronic cholesterol 691

accumulation, most animal models of MI involve only the surgical occlusion of the coronary 692

artery, absent the presence of chronic comorbidities or underlying genetic predispositions116. The 693

main surgical protocol to induce I/R or chronic MI in animals is coronary ligation, although 694

catheter-based approaches and coronary embolism are also choices116. To mimic multimorbid 695

conditions in patients with chronic ischemic HF, surgical-, diet-induced, or genetic animal 696

models can be performed in combination. 697

698

Models of Ischemic HF with CMDs 699

Various methods have been validated for inducing common CMDs such as hypertension, 700

diabetes, and obesity in animal models. These include dietary approaches (e.g., high-fat diet, 701

Western diet, or high-fat high-sugar diet), surgical techniques (e.g., TAC), pharmacological 702

agents (e.g., Ang II, streptozotocin [STZ]), and the use of mutant animals (e.g., Apoe or Ldlr- 703

knockout mice). These are used in combination with coronary artery ligation to mimic 704

comorbidities in ischemic HF116. For example, mice treated with STZ followed by coronary 705

ligation may mimic ischemic HF in patients with diabetes148,149, mice undergoing TAC surgery 706

followed by MI manifested more severe adverse myocardial remodeling and pronounced 707

HFrEF150. An animal model of cardiorenal syndrome was developed using coronary ligation in 708

spontaneously hypertensive rats combined with unilateral nephrectomy151. However, the report 709

did not provide detailed methodological information, imposing potential challenges in 710

reproducing the model. 711

712

Whereas combining MI with a single comorbidity is common, integrating multiple comorbidities 713

or surgeries into a single model remains rare. This is primarily due to the high mortality rates and 714

the complex interplay among them, which can complicate analysis of the experimental findings 715

and make it challenging to parse specific effects of each factor. 716

Models of Ischemic HF with Hyperlipidemia and Atherosclerosis 718

Apoe-knockout mice152 and Ldlr-knockout mice153 develop hyperlipidemia and spontaneous 719

atherosclerotic plaques when fed a high-fat diet (HFD)154. When subjected to chronic coronary 720

ligation, they serve as a model to study MI in the context of pre-existing hyperlipidemia and 721

atherosclerosis154. Similar animal strains include MI-prone WHHL rabbits (WHHLMI)155 and 722

SR-B1/LDLR double knockout mice156. These models mimic arterial atherosclerosis in patients, 723

spontaneous MI and peripheral artery disease (PAD). However, atherosclerosis develops slowly, 724

with heart attacks occurring after multiple months, and the variable heart damage that is induced 725

can lead to inconsistent phenotypes. 726

HFpEF with Multiple Cardiometabolic Comorbidities 728

Comparable to clinical phenotypes observed in patients, HFpEF models usually involve 2 or 729

more comorbidities centering around obesity and insulin resistance. Recent multifactorial models 730

have shown great promise for mimicking clinical complexity, and yet the models to date target- 731

specific HFpEF phenotypes, failing to capture the full heterogeneity of the HFpEF population. 732

Importantly, a perfect ‘one-size-fits-all’ preclinical model does not exist. Using diagnostic 733

criteria scores for patients, such as the H2FPEF126 and HFA-PEFF125, may help with validating 734

HFpEF models127,136. 735

Models of Unhealthy Lifestyle-induced CMDs 737

In preclinical models, unhealthy dietary patterns are mimicked by a HFD (>60% daily caloric 738

intake from fat) or by a Western diet (daily caloric intake of 36% fat and 36% sucrose). Utilizing 739

wild-type mice, rather than transgenic or strain-specific models, allows for a more accurate 740

representation of the general population with unhealthy lifestyles. Diet-based animal models 741

provide valuable insights into HF and associated CMDs in a broad context. However, severe 742

diabetes and advanced organ dysfunction are less commonly observed. 743

(1) HFD + L-NAME mice 745

The “two-hit” model replicates key lifestyle factors and clinical features associated with this 746

also mimics the genetic and molecular pathway alterations frequently observed in human HFpEF 749

diabetes are also present in this model. Moreover, AF, a prevalent occurrence in HF, is inducible 752

in 80% of cases in this model, coupled with left atrial enlargement, further mimicking human 753

Models Involving AF/MASLD: Future Directions 825

AF - a significant, and clinically important component of HF - has not been routinely 826

incorporated into the assessment of preclinical models of HFpEF. The "two-hit" model 827

combining HFD + L-NAME elicits an 80% incidence of inducible AF, but the mechanistic 828

relationship between AF and HF remains uncertain, mirroring the complex conundrum observed 829

in human diseases (See Box 1). Another significant challenge is the limited experimental 830

incorporation of MASLD into HFpEF animal models. MASLD is increasingly recognized as a 831

key factor in cardiometabolic health, sharing comorbidity patterns, including metabolic 832

inflammation, as in clinical HFpEF, as they often coexist and exacerbate each other's 833

progression. To date, MASLD has only been evaluated in a swine model treated with a 834

combination of WD and AB. In future models, MASLD should also be considered an important 835

component of the additional comorbidities in HFpEF models. 836

Aging Phenotype and Young HF Populations 838

Aging is among the greatest risk factors for CVD, impacting nearly all organ systems178,179. It is 839

often not studied as an independent factor in CVD owing to multiple technical challenges and 840

confounding factors, but can be easily examined alongside other comorbidities. Whereas elderly 841

patients often present with AF as a single comorbidity in clinical settings136, animal models 842

replicating this phenotype are limited. Fischer 344 rats exhibit age-related changes across 843

multiple organs, with myocardial progression from LVDD to clinical exercise intolerance, 844

ultimately culminating in left ventricular systolic dysfunction180,181. In a study of Fischer 344 rats 845

with HFpEF, atrial pacing was used to induce AF, resulting in increased AF vulnerability182. 846

However, the impact of AF on HFpEF in these models remains insufficiently explored. 847

Similarly, SAMP8 mice develop LVDD as early as six months of age but fail to exhibit a HFpEF 848

or AF phenotype183. The old hypertensive (OHT) dog induced by renal-wrapping is also a model 849

of hypertension in older animals but lacked evidence of bona fide HFpEF184-186.  Incorporating 850

older animals, with or without additional comorbidities, or extending the follow-up period for 851

younger animals, should be considered to potentially enhance the HFpEF phenotype. However, 852

incorporation of AF in preclinical models remains a major challenge. 853

The young patient population with HF typically comprises obese individuals with unhealthy 855

lifestyles (sedentary, unhealthy diet, smoking, etc.) with minimal comorbidities (commonly 856

hypertension and pre-diabetes). They have milder HF symptoms, lower NT-proBNP levels and 857

lower NYHA class144,145. Thus, HFpEF models incorporating multiple CMDs will likely help 858

illuminate the important features in this phenotype. 859

Limitations and perspectives for preclinical models incorporating HF comorbidities 861

HF is multifactorial and a biological challenge in which comorbidities contribute critically to the 862

pathophysiology of the clinical syndrome; unfortunately, this, in turn, complicates development 863

of preclinical animal models with clinical fidelity. Unsurprisingly, no single preclinical model 864

replicates the complete clinical complexity observed in HFpEF patients. Challenges exist in 865

several aspects, including difficulties in replicating the complex interactions among multiple 866

comorbid conditions and a lack of correlation between animals and humans in the biomarkers 867

used to assess disease progression and treatment efficacy. Translational failures also result from 868

differences between animals and humans in genetic background, molecular pathways, and 869

immune mechanisms. Notably, prevalent comorbidities of HF, such as AF and NASH, are 870

typically absent in existing multi-comorbidity preclinical animal models (See Box 1). 871

872

Beyond replicating clinical parameters and biomarkers, future animal models should also 873

prioritize molecular and genetic similarities HF patients. Furthermore, leveraging multiple 874

animal models in preclinical studies and therapeutic testing is strongly encouraged to capture the 875

diversity of HF phenotypes and ensure robust evaluation of novel mechanisms and potential 876

therapeutic targets. 877

Challenges of Multi-organ CKLM Clinical Trials 1050

1051

While multi-organ trials can generate meaningful evidence, they also face several challenges 1052

(Figure 5). One major challenge is that identifying appropriate patients with multi-organ disease 1053

is inherently complex. Traditional risk assessment tools, such as the Pooled Cohort Equations 1054

(PCE), do not account for the presence and severity of liver disease, which significantly impacts 1055

cardiovascular outcomes, morbidity, and mortality in patients with MASLD or MASH. For 1056

example, in 698 patients with MASLD from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis), 1057

PCE was suboptimal (AUROC: 0.67), predominantly underestimating risk in women within the 1058

lower to intermediate risk categories of MASLD229. Consequently, accurately identifying and 1059

stratifying such patients necessitates the collection of additional data and endpoints which 1060

increases the complexity and cost of multi-organ trials. 1061

1062

Incorporating patients with liver disease into cardiovascular and kidney trials is often met with 1063

hesitation due to concerns about drug metabolism and safety profiles. Many investigational drugs 1064

are metabolized in the liver, and patients with hepatic impairment may have altered 1065

pharmacokinetics which heightens the risk of adverse effects or hepatotoxicity189. This 1066

necessitates additional monitoring which complicates trial design and puts additional burden on 1067

the sponsor. The lack of standardized clinical guidelines for managing patients with overlapping 1068

conditions leads to variable treatment approaches and introduces heterogeneity into clinical 1069

trials. Patients with multi-organ diseases may receive different therapies based on local practices, 1070

specialist preferences, confusing and overlapping plans of care. This variability can confound 1071

trial results, making it challenging to attribute outcomes to the study drug rather than differences 1072

in standard care. 1073

1074

Traditional biopsy-based approaches for diagnosing and staging liver disease have a high screen 1075

failure rate of 70–90%. This means that for a trial aiming to enroll 1,000 patients, potentially 1076

>10,000 individuals may need to undergo liver biopsies. Given the serious morbidity and 1077

complication rate associated with liver biopsies, where ~1 patient may experience a near-death 1078

event per 1,000 procedures, this approach poses ethical concerns and contributes to patient 1079

reluctance to participate230. These liver biopsies are seldom used in routine clinical practice, 1080

primarily reserved for cases with diagnostic ambiguity, and are not recommended as standard 1081


<!-- Page 26 -->


diagnostic tools unless absolutely necessary94,231. Moreover, it may take up to five years to 1082

demonstrate any reduction in cirrhosis progression and even longer to observe changes in clinical 1083

events, making biopsy-based approaches impractical for timely trial outcomes. 1084

Establishing consensus on developing and validating clinically meaningful organ-specific 1086

efficacy and safety endpoints remains a contentious issue. For example, while liver biochemical 1087

tests or the FIB-4 index could be included in cardiovascular or kidney trials from a hepatology 1088

perspective, significant investment in liver-specific biomarkers is unlikely until there is a 1089

universally accepted case definition based on NITs232. Currently, there is no agreement on which 1090

NITs should be used, despite substantial investments and research in this area93,189. This lack of 1091

consensus hinders the ability to define meaningful changes in NITs and their clinical benefits, 1092

creating barriers to integrating liver endpoints into multi-organ trials. The different NITs have 1093

varying limitations; for instance, the FIB-4 score performs poorly in individuals over 65 years 1094

old and those with T2D, and has a high coefficient of variation. The ELF score offers better 1095

prognostic value with less variability but may not be widely accessible or cost-effective. 1096

Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) is considered the gold standard but is expensive and 1097

not feasible outside of specialized settings. 1098

Defining the optimal combination of biomarkers, imaging modalities, and hard clinical outcomes 1100

also remains a challenge. Future trials must balance the need for comprehensive data with the 1101

3) Meaningful Evidence 1236

There is a need to establish a consensus on what constitutes convincing evidence in multi-organ 1237

clinical trials. The key question in the context of multi-organ trials is how to design, execute, and 1238

interpret successful clinical trials that incorporate a multiplicity of endpoints. One potential 1239

approach is to employ causal inference frameworks in the design, execution, and interpretation 1240

of such complex trials to provide a systematic, step-by-step approach to pre-specifying study 1241

design and analysis plans242. Multi-organ clinical trials can encounter unique challenges, such as 1242

stringent regulatory requirements, lengthy follow-up periods for clinical endpoints, competing 1243

risks, invasive surrogate measures, and heterogeneous patient populations. To manage these 1244

complexities, innovative frameworks like the “Flexible Augmented Clinical Trial for Improved 1245

eVidence gEneration” (FACTIVE) have been developed243. FACTIVE designs bridge 1246

conventional phase III trials to a broader population, or different experimental conditions, that 1247

can be tailored to address a particular question243. FACTIVE enhances a core randomized trial by 1248

generating rigorous efficacy and safety data while integrating real-world elements typical of 1249

clinical practice. Briefly, FACTIVE design merges elements of a traditional randomized 1250

controlled trial with those of a real-world study243. Initially, FACTIVE sets up a core trial 1251

conducted under strict experimental conditions. This traditional segment serves as a rigorous 1252

control and minimizes variables that could affect the outcome. Concurrently, FACTIVE expands 1253

by incorporating an augmented part that includes real-world elements. This part of the trial is 1254

tailored to more closely resemble clinical practice, with a broader patient population and varied 1255

healthcare settings typical of routine clinical care243. This dual structure enables FACTIVE to 1256

produce robust evidence that is both scientifically valid and broadly applicable. 1257

and CKLM disease today in its totality. Notwithstanding all the challenges discussed, we need to 1314

consider how clinical trials can be conducted to include a broader cohort of patients with multi- 1315

organ diseases, and preclinical disease models can be selected to reflect current disease 1316

complexity. Clinical trials and preclinical disease models so designed may facilitate the efficient 1317

identification of therapies that benefit patients across multiple disease domains, aligning with 1318

real-world clinical settings (See Box 1). Collectively, for clinical trials, this also warrants a call 1319

to reduce reliance on invasive tests, develop reasonably likely surrogate endpoints, ensure 1320

broader demographic representation, and integrate AI-based tools to optimize patient selection 1321

and risk stratification. Multi-organ trials should include patients with modifiable disease, with 1322

consideration for practicality and retention, and assess comprehensive multi-organ parameters, 1323

along with a variety of endpoints. Overall, the traditional approach of HF epidemiology often 1324

focuses on individual cardiometabolic risk factors for overall HF risk. Instead, we propose a shift 1325

away from the siloed perspective and concerted systematic studies of shared mechanisms of 1326

extra-cardiac, multi-organ dysfunction.  Future research designs should integrate the concept of 1327

“common soil”, linking multi-organ readouts to comprehensively unravel the complexities of 1328

multimorbidity and heterogeneity across the clinical spectrum of HF. 1329
